title: Psalm 107: Let the Redeemed of the LORD Say So
summary: The redeemed, gathered from every direction, are called to give thanks for the LORD's enduring love. Four scenes follow: travelers lost in the desert, prisoners in darkness and chains, fools sick to the point of death, and sailors caught in a storm. In each, the people cry to the LORD in their trouble, he rescues them, and they are called to thank him. The psalm closes with a hymn about God reversing fortunes, turning rivers into desert and desert into springs, humbling nobles and lifting the needy, and it urges the wise to consider his loving devotion.
story: Psalm 107 opens Book V, the last book of the Psalter (Psalms 107 to 150). It answers the prayer that ended Book IV almost word for word. Psalm 106 closed with “gather us from the nations”; Psalm 107 begins with the redeemed “gathered from the lands”. Its first line even repeats the first line of Psalm 106. Book IV confessed the sin that led to exile; Book V begins with the people home and thanking God. From here the Psalter moves toward the psalms of ascent, the great Torah psalm (Psalm 119), and the closing hallelujahs, but it begins by telling stories of rescue that any returned exile, or any person in trouble, could recognize as their own.
historical:
The psalm has no heading. Verses 2 and 3, with their redeemed people gathered from east and west, north and south, most naturally reflect the return from exile after Cyrus of Persia allowed the exiled Jews to go home in 539/538 BC, and many scholars date the psalm, or at least its opening frame, to the period after that return. The four scenes that follow, however, are not specifically about exile: desert wanderers, prisoners, the sick, and sailors are types of human distress found in any age. Some scholars think an older thanksgiving liturgy, perhaps used when different groups brought thank offerings to the temple, was later given an introduction applying it to the returned exiles; others read the psalm as a single composition from the start.

In verse 3 the Hebrew literally pairs the north with the sea, and since the sea (the Mediterranean) lies to Israel's west, translators have usually adjusted it to south to complete the four directions. Verses 33 to 43 shift from the thanksgiving pattern to the style of wisdom teaching, and verse 42 closely resembles Job 5:16, which may show a shared wisdom tradition.
cultural:
Each scene draws on a real danger of ancient life. Caravans crossing the desert could lose the track and die of thirst far from any town, and a walled city was the image of safety and a settled home. Prisons were often pits or dungeons, dark places where captives were kept in chains, sometimes in forced labor; gates of bronze and bars of iron (verse 16) were the fortifications of great cities, and breaking them was the act of a conqueror. Illness was widely understood as connected to wrongdoing, and the psalm names these sufferers “fools” whose own rebellion brought them near “the gates of death” (verses 17 and 18).

Israelites were not a seafaring people, and the sea often stood in their poetry for chaos and danger. The picture of merchant sailors (verse 23) reflects the trade of the Phoenician coast, whose ships sailed the Mediterranean, and later Israelite shipping from ports such as Ezion-geber (1 Kings 9:26). The storm scene, with ships lifted to the heavens and sailors reeling like drunkards, describes what landlubbers most feared about the sea. The “sacrifices of thanksgiving” in verse 22 were the thank offerings brought to the temple after a rescue, accompanied by public testimony.
literary: The psalm is one of the most clearly structured in the Psalter. After the introduction (verses 1 to 3), four stanzas follow the same pattern: the distress described, then a first refrain, “Then they cried out to the LORD in their trouble”, then the rescue, then a second refrain calling them to give thanks “for His loving devotion and His wonders to the sons of men”, and finally a reason or a response (verses 4 to 9, 10 to 16, 17 to 22, 23 to 32). The refrains appear at verses 6, 13, 19, and 28, and at 8, 15, 21, and 31. Verses 33 to 42 drop the refrains and become a hymn about God's reversals, and verse 43 closes with a call to wisdom, much as Hosea 14:9 closes that prophet's book.

outline.t: Let the redeemed, gathered from the lands, give thanks
Wanderers in the desert led to a city
Prisoners in darkness freed from their chains
Fools near death healed by his word
Sailors in the storm brought to harbor
God reverses fortunes: deserts, springs, nobles, the needy
Let the wise consider the LORD's loving devotion

doctrines.note: The psalm offers four pictures of rescue: guidance for the lost, freedom for the imprisoned, healing for the sick, and calm for the storm-tossed. Each time the only thing the sufferers contribute is a cry for help.
“Then they cried out to the LORD in their trouble” is the hinge of every scene. Even those who suffered because of their own rebellion (verses 11 and 17) are heard when they cry out.

The closing hymn shows God governing nature and society alike, turning rivers into desert and desert into springs, humbling the proud and lifting the needy. The wise are those who notice his hand in these reversals.

words.note: Gaal, to redeem, the act of a kinsman-redeemer who bought back a relative from slavery or recovered family land (Leviticus 25; Ruth 4). Calling Israel “the redeemed of the LORD” pictures God as the family member who paid to bring them home.

Tsalmavet, deep darkness or the shadow of death. The word describes utter gloom, the darkness of a dungeon or of the grave. It appears in Psalm 23:4 and describes the prisoners' condition in verses 10 and 14.

Davar, word. In verse 20 God “sent forth His word and healed them”, picturing his word almost as a messenger sent on a mission (compare Isaiah 55:11). It contrasts with the fools of verse 11 who rebelled against the words of God.
Chesed, loving devotion or steadfast love. It frames the psalm, from verse 1 to the plural form in verse 43, and fills every refrain. Each rescue is presented as an act of God's covenant love.

christ: The Gospels describe Jesus doing what this psalm says the LORD does. When he calms a storm on the Sea of Galilee, the frightened disciples ask who this is, that even the wind and the sea obey him (Mark 4:35-41), a question that makes most sense against the background of this psalm, where only the LORD hushes the waves. Zechariah's song speaks of light dawning on those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death (Luke 1:79), language shared with verses 10 and 14 and with Isaiah 9:2. Jesus heals by his word, frees captives, feeds the hungry, and says that many will come from east and west to sit at table in the kingdom (Matthew 8:11). The psalm does not predict Jesus; it describes the God whom the Gospels show at work in him.

hard.q: If God rescues those who cry out, why do so many people cry out in trouble and seem not to be rescued?
hard.a: The psalm's four scenes all end in rescue, and many readers have known travelers who were not found, prisoners who were not freed, patients who were not healed, and sailors who did not reach harbor. The psalm is a thanksgiving song, written from the side of those who were rescued, and it does not claim to be a promise that every prayer will be answered in the same way. Other psalms, such as Psalm 88, speak from inside unanswered distress, and the Psalter keeps both voices. Some interpreters stress that the psalm's primary reference is the national rescue from exile; others read it as testimony that invites trust without guaranteeing an outcome. The closing verse calls the wise to consider the LORD's loving devotion, which suggests that understanding his ways takes reflection rather than a formula.

questions: Which of the four scenes (the lost, the imprisoned, the sick, the storm-tossed) best describes a time in your life, and what was your cry to God then?
Two groups in the psalm suffer because of their own rebellion and folly, and God still hears them. How does that shape the way you pray when you know you caused your own trouble?
The psalm says the redeemed should “say so”. Why do you think telling the story of a rescue matters, both for the teller and for those who hear it?
